title: Ask HN: I Need Advice
summary:
Hello HN.

I was laid off six months ago from my longest tenured job. Since then, I have been rotting. And I mean really rotting. I have been staying up late, sleeping in, skipping chores, neglecting my relationships, eating too much food, neglecting hygiene, and generally just being a bum. I have a nest egg that I had saved up for this exact situation, but it appears that it has just made me even lazier. I have not been applying to many jobs, maybe one per week. My main reason has been that I am afraid of interviewing and that my skills are not up to par.

I don't know what to do anymore. I need to kick myself into gear, but I am finding it incredibly difficult. I'm not looking for pity, just some assistance from the brain trust here at HN.

Thank you for reading.

title: Ask HN: Advise on monetization model for my freemium app wanted
summary:
I'm an indie app dev and looking for some conceptual help with one of my freemium apps. I'm thinking about completely restructuring the business model i.e. the placement of the paywall and what amount of content stays free and what'll move behind the paywall.

To be clear: This isn't meant to be a hidden advertisement for my app. I won't even tell the name (if not explicitly asked for in the comments).

Just for enough context: It's a low-stimulating, stress-free coloring game for children - especially for neurodivergent ones (e.g. ADHD, autism). There are no ads in the app. Images are colored by simple taps and swipes. No mistakes possible.

---

The situation: The app is around 1 year old (in the Play Store; it's in review for the App Store rn). It had 3.5 k installs. There's a premium in-app purchase - one-time, not a subscription. It costs 6 $. During the lifetime of the app an amazing amount of 4 users bought premium. That's a conversion rate of ~0.1 %. And also the app only received 5 ratings.

The app is divided into "worlds": Themed level packs with 10 levels each. One level can be finished in 10 - 30 seconds. There are 20 worlds rn. Every second world is a "premium world" that can only be played by premium users - besides the first level, which is free for everyone as a teaser. I regularly add new worlds (always 1 free and 1 premium together). Premium also unlocks the possibility to use own images for coloring.

The app has a structural problem with the paywall as well as the ratings prompt: The game is played by children (4 to 12). The paywall is shown for the first time after 11 levels have been played. At that time the device is most likely in the hands of a child - but the parents have the money, obviously. Similar for the ratings prompt: It is passive rn buried in the settings screen where rarely anybody sees it. And with 110 levels being available for free, there's probably no need at all to buy more content.

---

My plan for the new structure:

1. Remove the "zipper" pattern of alternating free and premium worlds. 2. World 1 and 2 will be free to play. 3. All remaining worlds will be premium (maybe I'll keep the first level of each world free as a teaser). 4. Put an info for parents right before the first level that's being played (hoping/expecting that the parents will still have the device in hands at that time or are at least nearby). The info will explain the model (2 free worlds, no ads, no tracking, no subscriptions etc. 20 worlds with 200 levels unlockable for 6 $). 5. Two buttons below: "test for free" and "unlock everything now".

---

My questions for you (you don't need to answer all to help me):

1. What do you think about my planned model? Do you think it will work/convert? 2. Do you think it's a fair model? An acceptable price? 3. Where (or probably rather "when") would you show a rating prompt? 4. Would you keep level 1 of each world free? There are different mechanics how an image can be colored (tied to the world), so if I don't keep every first level free, some mechanics can never be experienced before buying premium. 5. Would you put the two best (most fun) mechanics in the first two free worlds to encourage premium buys? Or rather spare them for premium?

Thanks so much to everyone who read this and is willing to help me out with some answers!

title: Watch Apple slowly become just another computer company
summary:
1. no one wants a folding iphone 2. no one wants touch on the mac

stop blindly listening to journalists and have some taste.

i have a UX maxim with a ton of evidence behind it that no one seems to talk about:

if a product you're releasing has worse ergonomics that what currently exists, it WON'T WORK. evidence:

1. the wii -> was a success itself but couldn't go to a next generation because having static controllers is more ergonomic than the waving around gimmick 2. the touchbar -> looking at the small screen is less ergonomic than muscle memory 3. butterfly keyboard 4. touch keyboards on laptops -> no muscle memory 5. stylus 6. VR (and especially the apple vision which is extremely heavy) 7. every voice agent device ever -> rabbit r1, humane pin, muse device and whatever openai has in mind won't work. voice is very limiting in a ton of situations where it would render the device useless. 8. car touchscreens for everything instead of physical buttons (we haven't gone past this yet) 9. 3d tvs

the list goes on.

the proof that this is a law of UX is that the opposite is also true:

1. agents are better than UIs -> having an agent that knows a ton about me, how i like to work and can connect to UIs that are inconsistent and buggy is fantastic and that's why everyone's using them. 2. automatic transmission (unless you're an enthusiast) 3. phone aspect ratios converging (remember early 2000 where all phones were completely different with zero interchangeability?) 4. mice > trackpad 5. airpods 6. keyless car entry 7. tab autocomplete 8. apple pay 9. rolling luggage

touch on a laptop is the most unergonomic thing someone could come up with. how is it easier to lift your arm from the resting position where the trackpad is to touch the same thing the trackpad could touch?

folding phones are a worse version of the ipad, much worse version of the mac, and much worse version of the regular iphone. people don't want to work on their phones.

title: Ask HN: What happened to our collective ethos?
summary:
I’m an outsider to both Silicon Valley and enterprise IT; I’m just a freelance consultant and web host plying my trade in the suburbs of Charlotte. But I have generally presumed that we all share a common nostalgic ideal rooted in the memories and stories of Bell Labs, Xerox PARC, and their unbound, open-ended exploration of science, technology, and the limits of their imaginations. I’ve been told that the economic and regulatory conditions that allowed these monuments to human endeavor ultimately shifted, monopolies were broken up, assets were sold off, and it ultimately served as the incubator for the modern technology industry.

But we’ve since seen companies emerge with market dominance and wealth that the Bell Group could only dream about, who presided over a decade and a half of near-zero interest rates. None of whom elected to establish/fund public-facing research campuses stuffed with Nobel laureates conducting their own frontier research departments. What’s worse, most of them instead chose to turn their oligopolies towards seeking to control the media and political process, privatizing what was left of America’s public aerospace programs, gatekeeping research and development, and subsidizing their further encroachments with the resulting government contracts.

How are these the people we granted so much power and influence to? Was it simply that Silicon Valley was captured by the financial industry? Was the origin story always a convenient myth, that nobody ever actually took seriously, or objected to when it was cynically exploited by the patently disingenuous and greedy CEOs who have, without exception, acted in the worst interests of their users, society, and the planet? Just the base selfishness of human nature?

Were the research and development labs of the post-war American era just a flash in the pan, or could Silicon Valley someday rediscover its lost soul? I’d reckon we’d all be better off for it, but I am also concerned that I simply fell the for the marketing hype, and there never was the altruistic spirit of innovation I’d always imagined.

title: A garbage collector for LLM context windows, written in Rust
summary:
Hi HN,

Like many of you, I spend a lot of time coding with Codex and switching between cloud and local models.

As a software engineer, something I never understood, and honestly hated—was `/compact` and the way it’s designed. On local models my GPU screams, and after a few hours prefill takes 2 to 3 minutes per turn. On cloud models, as the context grows, the model starts getting noticeably dumber. IMHO the root problem is context bloat and the fact that compaction destroys the quality of the model's working memory.

Looking under the hood and studying how attention works, I learned that memory in modern harnesses is basically "append-only." and attention on long context becames less effective due to the attenttion dead zone. So you end up having in the context thousands of lines of old compiler dumps and duplicate file reads sitting there rent free destroying the agent's attention.

Having an LLM write a summary of your conversation and blowing away your KV-cache makes no engineering sense imho especially on local models where prompt prefill latency is critical (and on cloud models where you lose prompt-cache discounts).

So I built a piece of software called *contextWatcher* (or *`cw`* for friends and family).

It’s a Rust proxy that runs locally on CPU ( in less than 2ms), and gives:

1. Shadow-Deduplication: Computes BLAKE3 hashes of file reads. If the agent reads for example a file like `src/main.rs` at Turn 2, edits it at Turn 5, and reads it again at Turn 9, Turns 2 and 5 are replaced with 1-line pointer stubs. Only the latest version stays in context. 2. Surgical Tool Pruning: Truncates runaway compiler output (keeping the tool_call_id, invocation, and the panic/exit trace intact) so schemas and error context never break. 3. Tail Rule Pinning: Dynamically mirrors critical system constraints (from AGENTS.md) right above the latest user prompt, pulling them out of the middle attention dead-zone without invalidating the cached prefix. 4. Swarm Prefix Multiplexing: When multiple subagents collaborate on the same workspace, cw extracts the shared root prefix (tools, rules, system prompt) so local inference engines (llama.cpp / vLLM) only keep one copy in VRAM. 5. Cache Preservation: Operates without rewriting the stable prefix, keeping prompt caching intact.

On my local dual AMD GPU (Radeon Instinct Mi50 32GB) setup with a ~28k context session, cleaning out this dead weight dropped prompt prefill from ~170 seconds down to ~1.6 seconds and unlike fuzzy compaction, ground-truth code stayed 100% intact and all unit tests passed.

It's open source (MIT / Apache-2.0) and installs via a one-liner: ```curl -fsSL https://constant-labs.com/cw-install.sh | sh```

Repo: https://github.com/GionaGranchelli/context-watcher

For me and my setup worked pretty well, and I am satisfied with the result I get, I am really curious to see other people testing it and giving me an honest feedback on the tool and the approach

Hi HN,

Like many of you, I spend a lot of time coding with Codex and switching between cloud and local models.

As a software engineer, something I never understood, and honestly hated—was `/compact` and the way it’s designed. On local models my GPU screams, and after a few hours prefill takes 2 to 3 minutes per turn. On cloud models, as the context grows, the model starts getting noticeably dumber. IMHO the root problem is context bloat and the fact that compaction destroys the quality of the model's working memory.

Looking under the hood and studying how attention works, I learned that memory in modern harnesses is basically "append-only." and attention on long context becames less effective due to the attenttion dead zone. So you end up having in the context thousands of lines of old compiler dumps and duplicate file reads sitting there rent free destroying the agent's attention.

Having an LLM write a summary of your conversation and blowing away your KV-cache makes no engineering sense imho especially on local models where prompt prefill latency is critical (and on cloud models where you lose prompt-cache discounts).

So I built a piece of software called *contextWatcher* (or *`cw`* for friends and family).

It’s a Rust proxy that runs locally on CPU ( in less than 2ms), and gives:

1. Shadow-Deduplication: Computes BLAKE3 hashes of file reads. If the agent reads for example a file like `src/main.rs` at Turn 2, edits it at Turn 5, and reads it again at Turn 9, Turns 2 and 5 are replaced with 1-line pointer stubs. Only the latest version stays in context. 2. Surgical Tool Pruning: Truncates runaway compiler output (keeping the tool_call_id, invocation, and the panic/exit trace intact) so schemas and error context never break. 3. Tail Rule Pinning: Dynamically mirrors critical system constraints (from AGENTS.md) right above the latest user prompt, pulling them out of the middle attention dead-zone without invalidating the cached prefix. 4. Swarm Prefix Multiplexing: When multiple subagents collaborate on the same workspace, cw extracts the shared root prefix (tools, rules, system prompt) so local inference engines (llama.cpp / vLLM) only keep one copy in VRAM. 5. Cache Preservation: Operates without rewriting the stable prefix, keeping prompt caching intact.

On my local dual AMD GPU (Radeon Instinct Mi50 32GB) setup with a ~28k context session, cleaning out this dead weight dropped prompt prefill from ~170 seconds down to ~1.6 seconds and unlike fuzzy compaction, ground-truth code stayed 100% intact and all unit tests passed.

It's open source (MIT / Apache-2.0) and installs via a one-liner: ```curl -fsSL https://constant-labs.com/cw-install.sh | sh```

Repo: https://github.com/GionaGranchelli/context-watcher

For me and my setup worked pretty well, and I am satisfied with the result I get, I am really curious to see other people testing it and giving me an honest feedback on the tool and the approach
